# Where these bytes came from

A test for a legacy encoding is only worth something if it starts from bytes. Start from characters and you have already assumed the answer to the only question being asked, which is what the bytes meant. So the bytes are here, one file per document, and the `.txt` beside each one is what `phoi` makes of it. The `.txt` files are generated and can be rewritten with `go test ./phoi -update`. The `.bytes` files are not generated by anything and are never rewritten.

Two of these are independent facts about an encoding and the rest are gao agreeing with itself. Which is which matters more than how many there are, so it is written out below rather than left to be worked out from the file names.

## pho-co-ha-noi.tcvn3.bytes

A real page, and the only one here that is. It is the document in `normalize/testdata/font-cu.in`, a Hanoi street piece from 1998 that reached the corpus as mojibake, and mojibake is reversible: a page in TCVN3 read as windows-1252 comes out as characters that map back to the bytes one for one, which is what `normalize.Text` undoes. So these are the bytes that were on the wire. `iconv -f TCVN5712-1` will not read this file back on macOS, because that decoder returns NUL for the ASCII range there, and the encoder is the direction it is right in.

## song-hong.\*.bytes

One paragraph of real Vietnamese, the Red River entry in `normalize/testdata/bach-khoa.out`, written out in all six encodings. It has no capital with a mark on it, which is what lets TCVN3 carry it: capitals in that encoding live in a second font rather than in the file.

The TCVN3 and VISCII files were produced by iconv:

    iconv -f UTF-8 -t TCVN5712-1 paragraph.txt > song-hong.tcvn3.bytes
    iconv -f UTF-8 -t VISCII     paragraph.txt > song-hong.viscii.bytes

iconv carries its own tables and did not get them from here, so those two files are a check on the tables in `legacy_table.go` rather than a copy of them. The VNI, VPS and BK HCM files were written from gao's own tables, because no second implementation of those encodings exists to write them. They prove that the detector picks each one out of six candidates that all decode these bytes to Vietnamese letters, and they prove nothing about whether the tables are right.

All six come out as the same text, which is the point of the set.

## cong-bao.viscii.bytes

An official document header, in capitals, encoded by iconv and read back by iconv. The body was written for this test rather than taken from a real gazette. It is here for the capitals: the documents above have none with marks on them, and the capitals are where three of these encodings put the five codes windows-1252 leaves undefined. Six bytes of this file are in that range, and a decoder that returns the replacement character for them, as most of them do, loses ẮẾỐ and never says so.

## viscii.iconv and tcvn5712-1.iconv

Not documents. Each of the 134 letters of Vietnamese and the bytes iconv encodes it as, one to a line, generated once by asking iconv for each letter in turn. They are committed so that the check runs on a machine with no iconv on it, which is every machine the tests run on.

They are the third source for the two encodings that have one, after UniKey's vnconv and vnkey. The test reads them back against the tables in `legacy_table.go` and pins three counts per encoding: the codes both define, the codes iconv defines above 0x80 and gao leaves empty, and the letters iconv puts below 0x80, which gao does not read. Finding a code where the two disagree outright is what the file is for. It has happened once so far, on VISCII 0xa0.
